Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Vignette:
Ravi, a 58-year-old product manager, sat in his suburban home, the weight of the world pressing down on his shoulders. It had been years since the harrowing experience that turned his life upside down, yet the echoes of that trauma still reverberated through his daily existence. He had once been a vibrant man, filled with ambition and laughter, but now he often felt like a ghost of his former self, haunted by memories he couldn’t escape.

The incident that altered his reality occurred during a politically charged time in his home country. Ravi had been in the wrong place at the wrong time, a victim of brutality that left him imprisoned, tortured, and forever changed. The sharp sounds of incomprehensible chatter had been the backdrop to his suffering, muffled voices discussing his fate in a language he barely understood. Even now, years later, those sounds sent waves of anxiety crashing over him when he encountered crowds or places bustling with activity. Ravi found himself gripped by panic, his heart racing, and dizziness overwhelming him as memories flooded back uninvited.

As he navigated his daily life, Ravi learned to exist in a state of constant vigilance. He would often catch himself scanning his surroundings, checking for potential threats. The sirens of nearby emergency vehicles became a trigger, a stark reminder of the chaos he had endured. On one particularly difficult night, he lay in bed, wide awake, straining to hear the sounds of the world outside. Every siren that wailed in the distance felt like a personal attack, pulling him back into a past he desperately wished to forget. In that moment, he would wake up startled, heart racing, needing to ensure he was still safe, that no one was coming to take him away again.

Ravi’s coping mechanisms evolved as he tried to shield himself from potential stressors. He avoided situations that could bring about anxiety, meticulously planning his outings to ensure he didn’t encounter anything that might trigger his overwhelming fear. Even discussions at work about product launches or team shifts felt too daunting; he often excused himself, claiming he had pressing matters to attend to. His colleagues began to notice his withdrawal, but Ravi was certain that if he stayed away from stressful environments, he could protect himself from the turmoil brewing within.

He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, a notion that seeped into his interactions with others. Ravi found it hard to trust anyone, certain that people could not be relied upon. The lingering thought that there was something inherently wrong with him, something that had brought about his suffering, gnawed at him relentlessly. It was a conviction that made it difficult to form new relationships or to enjoy the company of old friends. His wife, Mira, often expressed concern, but he could only offer her a distant smile, fearing that opening up would expose him to more hurt. He had become adept at wearing a mask, but inside he felt utterly alone.

Even the sight of military or police uniforms sent him spiraling into distress. The sight of a uniformed officer in a restaurant would send him into a panic, a rush of memories flooding back with each pinstripes and badge. It was a reminder of the authority figures who had once stripped him of his humanity, leaving him vulnerable and afraid. He would often leave such places abruptly, much to Mira’s confusion, who struggled to understand the depth of his pain.

Having spent years in this cycle of avoidance and hyper-vigilance, Ravi finally reached a breaking point. He realized that his avoidance strategies were costing him his marriage and his job. His relationship with Mira had become strained, filled with unspoken words and missed connections. He recognized the toll his fears had taken on his life; he could no longer bear the isolation he felt. One afternoon, after a particularly harrowing episode triggered by a loud noise from the street, he sat down with Mira and confessed the turmoil that had gripped him for so long. It was a moment of vulnerability that he had been avoiding, but it felt necessary.

What frightened him most was the thought of remaining trapped in this cycle. He yearned for relief, for the chance to reclaim his life and trust again. It was in that moment of honesty that he decided to seek help, hoping to find a way to navigate the shadows of his past and reclaim the joy he once felt. As he prepared for his first therapy appointment, Ravi felt a flicker of hope amid his fear, a glimmer that perhaps, just perhaps, there was a path forward.
